musical.title: The Wizard of Oz
musical.book_by: John Kane (original), adapted by various (RSC version by John Kane for the Royal Shakespeare Company)
musical.based_on: The Wonderful Wizard of Oz by L. Frank Baum and the 1939 MGM film
musical.setting: Kansas and the Land of Oz
musical.vocal_style: Classic musical theatre with legit soprano lead, character voices, and ensemble harmony
musical.license_holder: Tams-Witmark / Concord Theatricals (RSC version) or R&H Theatricals (Andrew Lloyd Webber version)
musical.synopsis: Young Dorothy Gale is swept away from her Kansas farm by a tornado into the magical Land of Oz. To find her way home, she must follow the Yellow Brick Road to the Emerald City and seek the help of the great and powerful Wizard. Along the way, she befriends a Scarecrow who wants a brain, a Tin Man who wants a heart, and a Cowardly Lion who wants courage. Together they face the Wicked Witch of the West, discover the Wizard's true nature, and learn that the qualities they sought were within them all along.

roles.name: Dorothy Gale
roles.description: A brave, kind-hearted Kansas farm girl who is swept into Oz by a tornado. Dorothy is the emotional centre of the entire show — earnest, curious, determined, and deeply loyal to her friends. She carries nearly every scene and must connect with both child and adult audiences.

vocal.tessitura: Middle to upper register, sustained legit singing
vocal.style_notes: Pure, clear legit soprano with emotional vulnerability. 'Over the Rainbow' requires sustained phrasing, breath control, and genuine emotional depth. Must sound youthful but vocally mature.

dance.stamina: High — onstage nearly the entire show
dance.notes: The Yellow Brick Road sequences require coordinated movement with trio. Must move naturally through many set transitions and maintain energy throughout.

acting.emotional_range: Very wide — homesickness, wonder, fear, determination, joy, grief, love
acting.notes: Must be utterly sincere without being saccharine. Dorothy's journey is the audience's journey — she needs to carry genuine emotional weight while remaining accessible to children. The Kansas/Oz contrast demands range.

special_skills: Carrying emotional arc of entire show

casting_insights.why: Dorothy is the quintessential leading role — onstage almost continuously, sings the most iconic song in musical theatre history, and carries the entire emotional arc. This role builds every skill simultaneously.
casting_insights.common_casting: Young women with genuine warmth, clear soprano voices, and natural likability. Often cast younger (teens to early 20s) for community/school productions.
casting_insights.standout_opportunity: 'Over the Rainbow' is one of the most recognizable songs ever written. A truly great Dorothy can make an audience weep with this single number.

challenge_areas: Sustaining energy across 2+ hour show
Making iconic role feel fresh and personal
Balancing sincerity with avoiding sentimentality
Vocal stamina for legit singing throughout
recommended_for: Young sopranos ready for their first major lead
Performers with strong emotional connection
Singers who excel in legit/classical style
Actors who connect naturally with family audiences

what_directors_look_for: Genuine warmth and likability from the first moment
Clean, clear soprano voice with emotional depth
Ability to carry 'Over the Rainbow' with fresh sincerity
Natural chemistry with scene partners
Physical stamina and energy
common_mistakes: Imitating Judy Garland instead of finding own interpretation
Playing Dorothy as too young or too mature
Over-singing 'Over the Rainbow' — it needs simplicity
Lacking genuine emotional stakes in the Kansas scenes
tips: Make Dorothy YOUR Dorothy — directors have seen every Judy impression
The Kansas scenes set up everything — invest fully in the homesickness
Show range by contrasting wonder in Oz with determination against the Witch
Practice sustaining energy and vocal stamina for the full run

key_songs.title: Over the Rainbow
key_songs.notes: THE iconic song. Requires sustained legit phrasing, emotional vulnerability, and simplicity. Less is more.

key_songs.title: Follow the Yellow Brick Road / We're Off to See the Wizard
key_songs.notes: Joyful travelling number with Scarecrow, Tin Man, and Lion. Must maintain energy and character.

key_songs.title: Merry Old Land of Oz
key_songs.notes: Ensemble celebration in Emerald City. Dorothy participates with full cast.

roles.name: Scarecrow
roles.description: A lovable, floppy scarecrow who wants a brain. The Scarecrow is Dorothy's first friend in Oz and often the comic heart of the show. He is physically inventive, warm-hearted, and ironically the smartest of the trio. Typically doubled with Hunk in Kansas.

vocal.tessitura: Mid-range, conversational singing with character inflection
vocal.style_notes: Character voice with warmth. Needs to blend well in trio/quartet numbers. Comedy timing in vocal delivery is more important than vocal power.

dance.notes: The Scarecrow is defined by movement. Must create convincing floppy, boneless physicality while maintaining enough control for choreography. 'If I Only Had a Brain' typically features extended physical comedy/dance.

acting.emotional_range: Moderate — comedy to genuine tenderness in farewell scene
acting.notes: Physical comedy is paramount. Must sustain distinctive physicality for the entire show without it becoming gimmicky. The farewell with Dorothy needs genuine emotional weight.

casting_insights.why: The Scarecrow is often the audience favourite due to the physical comedy. This role develops physical theatre skills enormously and allows a performer to build a complete character through movement. The farewell scene tests emotional depth.
casting_insights.common_casting: Physically agile performers with strong comedy instincts. Often cast with dancers or physical theatre specialists who can sustain floppy physicality.
casting_insights.standout_opportunity: 'If I Only Had a Brain' is a showstopper when the physicality is inventive. A great Scarecrow steals scenes without upstaging Dorothy.

skills_developed: Sustained character physicality over full show
challenge_areas: Maintaining floppy physicality without injury
Finding fresh physical choices for iconic role
Balancing comedy with genuine heart
Sustaining energy in physically demanding role
recommended_for: Physical theatre enthusiasts
Performers wanting to develop comedy skills
Dancers looking to expand into character work
Actors who love building characters through movement

what_directors_look_for: Inventive, committed physicality from the first moment
Warmth and likability beneath the comedy
Ability to sustain character movement without flagging
Natural chemistry and generosity with scene partners
Vocal clarity and comedy timing
common_mistakes: Playing the Scarecrow as stupid rather than lovably naive
Physicality that looks rehearsed rather than spontaneous
Overdoing comedy at the expense of heart
Neglecting the vocal requirements of the role
tips: Develop a specific physical vocabulary — how does YOUR scarecrow move?
Study physical comedians (Buster Keaton, Charlie Chaplin) for inspiration
The straw stuffing affects everything — how do you sit, stand, walk, fall?
Show emotional depth in the farewell — this is what elevates good to great

key_songs.title: If I Only Had a Brain
key_songs.notes: Signature number combining character singing with extended physical comedy. The dance break is the highlight.

key_songs.title: We're Off to See the Wizard
key_songs.notes: Recurring travelling number with Dorothy and companions.

key_songs.title: Merry Old Land of Oz
key_songs.notes: Full company number in the Emerald City.

roles.name: Tin Man
roles.description: A rusted tin woodsman who longs for a heart. Despite claiming he cannot feel emotions, the Tin Man is the most emotional of the trio — easily moved to tears and deeply caring. His journey is about recognising the love he already possesses. Typically doubled with Hickory in Kansas.

vocal.tessitura: Mid-range baritone with warm, emotional quality
vocal.style_notes: Warm, resonant tone that conveys longing and tenderness. 'If I Only Had a Heart' needs genuine emotional ache. Must blend in trio harmonies.

dance.stamina: Moderate — costume can be physically restrictive
dance.notes: Must create convincing mechanical/stiff movement while still being endearing. The costume significantly restricts movement, so all choreography must work within those constraints. Oil can scene is key physical comedy moment.

acting.emotional_range: Wide — the irony is he's the MOST emotional character despite wanting a heart
acting.notes: The comedy comes from the contrast between claiming to have no heart and being overwhelmingly emotional. Must play genuine tenderness without sentimentality. Crying/emotional moments need to land.

casting_insights.why: A beloved role that teaches performers to act through heavy costume/makeup restrictions. The Tin Man develops emotional authenticity and the ability to convey character through limited physical means — invaluable skills.
casting_insights.common_casting: Warm baritones with natural emotional expressiveness. Actors who can convey feeling through voice and eyes when body is restricted by costume.
casting_insights.standout_opportunity: The oil can/unfreezing scene is a wonderful comic moment, and the farewell with Dorothy can be genuinely moving.

skills_developed: Vocal expressiveness when physical expression is limited
Ensemble work and scene partner generosity
challenge_areas: Heavy costume management (heat, visibility, mobility)
Projecting emotion through makeup/mask
Maintaining vocal quality in restrictive costume
Finding variety within mechanical movement
recommended_for: Baritones seeking iconic character roles
Performers wanting to develop emotional range
Actors interested in character work with physical constraints
Those building experience with heavy costume/makeup work

what_directors_look_for: Warm, resonant singing voice with emotional depth
Natural tenderness and likability
Understanding of physical comedy within constraints
Ability to convey emotion through voice and eyes
Good ensemble chemistry
common_mistakes: Playing the mechanical movement as robotic rather than rusty
Overplaying the crying — it should be endearing, not annoying
Neglecting the warmth that makes the irony work
Not considering the practical challenges of the costume
tips: Study how emotion reads when your body can't move freely — it's all in the voice and eyes
The irony IS the character: he already has the biggest heart of anyone
Practice singing with restricted movement — you'll need this skill
Make the farewell with Dorothy genuinely moving

key_songs.title: If I Only Had a Heart
key_songs.notes: Tender, longing ballad. Must convey genuine emotional ache while managing mechanical physicality.

key_songs.title: We're Off to See the Wizard
key_songs.notes: Recurring group number. Must integrate mechanical movement into the choreography.

key_songs.title: Merry Old Land of Oz
key_songs.notes: Full company celebration.

roles.name: Cowardly Lion
roles.description: A timid, theatrical lion who desperately wants courage. The Lion is the biggest comedy role in the show — a bombastic, dramatic personality masking deep insecurity. He provides much of the second-act energy and his courage arc is both funny and genuinely touching. Typically doubled with Zeke in Kansas.

vocal.tessitura: Mid-range with strong character voice, big personality in delivery
vocal.style_notes: Character voice with comedic flair. Needs vocal variety — bluster, whimpering, bravado, and genuine tenderness. 'If I Only Had the Nerve' is a comedy number that needs vocal personality.

dance.stamina: Moderate to high — big physical performance in costume
dance.notes: The Lion is physically expressive — cowering, puffing up, sneaking, trembling. Heavy lion costume/suit requires stamina. Movement should be big and expressive.

acting.emotional_range: Wide — terror, bravado, vulnerability, genuine courage
acting.notes: The premier comedy role. Must have impeccable timing and the ability to get big laughs while still making the audience root for the character. The moment of genuine courage needs to land after all the comedy.

casting_insights.why: The Lion is the audience-favourite comedy role and often gets the biggest laughs of the night. This role develops comedy chops, character voice work, and the crucial skill of balancing big comedy with genuine heart.
casting_insights.common_casting: Big personality performers with strong comedy instincts. Often cast with larger-framed actors who can be physically imposing yet endearingly cowardly.
casting_insights.standout_opportunity: 'If I Only Had the Nerve' and the 'King of the Forest' sequence are guaranteed crowd-pleasers. A great Lion can dominate every scene he's in.

challenge_areas: Not overplaying comedy at expense of story
Performing in heavy, hot costume
Finding genuine courage moment after sustained comedy
Supporting Dorothy's arc while getting big laughs
recommended_for: Comedic performers ready for a signature role
Actors wanting to develop character comedy
Performers who need to learn balancing laughs with heart
Those building comedy confidence in a forgiving role

what_directors_look_for: Strong comedy instincts and timing
Big, expressive personality that fills the stage
Character voice variety (bluster vs whimper vs genuine)
Ability to shift from comedy to genuine emotion
Physical expressiveness and stamina
common_mistakes: Making the Lion one-note — all cowardice, no variety
Overdoing it so much that the character becomes annoying
Ignoring the genuine emotional arc beneath the comedy
Not considering the physical demands of the costume
tips: The comedy comes from the contrast between bravado and cowardice — play BOTH
Study great comic actors who balance big comedy with real heart
The courage moment near the end only works if we've believed the cowardice
'King of the Forest' is your moment to SHINE — make it theatrical and fun

key_songs.title: If I Only Had the Nerve
key_songs.notes: Big comedy number. Needs vocal personality, physical comedy, and audience engagement.

key_songs.title: King of the Forest
key_songs.notes: Bravado sequence where Lion gets to be theatrical and commanding — before falling apart.

key_songs.title: We're Off to See the Wizard
key_songs.notes: Recurring group number with full quartet.

roles.name: Wicked Witch of the West
roles.description: The terrifying, cackling villain of Oz. The Wicked Witch is pure theatrical evil — commanding, menacing, and deliciously over-the-top. She commands the Winged Monkeys, threatens Dorothy and her friends, and meets a spectacular end. Despite limited stage time, she dominates every scene she appears in. Typically doubled with Miss Gulch in Kansas.

vocal.tessitura: Lower mezzo with powerful, cutting belt for dramatic moments
vocal.style_notes: Character voice — cackling, sneering, commanding. Vocal power matters more than beauty. Must cut through ensemble and be terrifying. Some versions include extended musical passages.

dance.stamina: Low to moderate — intense scenes but with offstage recovery time
dance.notes: Minimal dance but maximum physical presence. Every movement must be deliberate and menacing. The melting scene requires physical commitment.

acting.emotional_range: Focused — rage, cunning, malice, with occasional dark humor
acting.notes: Must dominate every scene despite limited time onstage. The Witch needs to genuinely frighten younger audience members while remaining theatrical enough for adults to enjoy. The line between scary and campy is the sweet spot.

casting_insights.why: Despite only 20% stage time, the Wicked Witch is one of the most memorable roles in the show. Every entrance is an event. This role teaches maximum impact with minimum time — a masterclass in theatrical presence.
casting_insights.common_casting: Powerful female performers with commanding presence and strong character voice. Often cast with experienced actresses who can terrify and entertain simultaneously.
casting_insights.standout_opportunity: Every single appearance is a star turn. The cackle, the threats, the melting — all iconic moments that audiences remember forever.

skills_developed: Maximum impact in limited stage time
challenge_areas: Finding the right balance of scary and entertaining
Making the role your own when everyone knows the character
Green makeup management across multiple shows
Quick transitions between Gulch and Witch
recommended_for: Experienced performers wanting a villainous showcase
Actors developing stage presence and command
Those who want maximum impact in a beloved show
Character actresses with powerful voices

what_directors_look_for: Commanding presence that fills the room immediately
A distinctive, powerful cackle
Ability to balance genuine menace with theatrical entertainment
Strong character voice and vocal projection
Physical authority and deliberate movement
common_mistakes: Going full camp without any genuine threat
Copying Margaret Hamilton too closely
Neglecting Miss Gulch — she should foreshadow the Witch
A weak or unconvincing cackle
tips: Develop YOUR cackle — practice until it's second nature and always consistent
Miss Gulch and the Witch should rhyme but not be identical
Less is more with movement — a slow, deliberate Witch is scarier than a frantic one
Find moments of dark humour — the best Witches make the audience laugh AND flinch

key_songs.title: Red Shoes Blues / Witch scenes
key_songs.notes: Musical underscoring for entrances and confrontations. Some versions include a full Witch number.

key_songs.title: Poppies/Jitterbug sequence
key_songs.notes: The Witch's magical assault. Some versions include the cut 'Jitterbug' number.

roles.name: Glinda the Good Witch
roles.description: The beautiful, sparkling Good Witch of the North (or South, depending on version). Glinda is warm, gracious, ethereal, and slightly mysterious — she guides Dorothy at key moments and ultimately reveals that Dorothy always had the power to go home. A fairy godmother figure who bookends the Oz narrative.

vocal.style_notes: Pure, ethereal soprano with warmth. Must sound otherworldly and reassuring. Some versions include a full Glinda number; others are primarily dialogue with underscoring.

dance.stamina: Low — appears in key scenes but not continuously
dance.notes: Glinda moves with grace and poise. Often makes dramatic entrances (bubble, light effect). Movement should feel effortless and magical.

acting.emotional_range: Moderate — warmth, wisdom, gentle authority, reassurance
acting.notes: Must convey genuine warmth and wisdom. Glinda's key moments — the arrival, the advice, and the revelation about the ruby slippers — need to feel genuinely magical and moving.

casting_insights.why: Glinda is a lovely, visible role with limited demands. Perfect for a soprano wanting a named role without the pressure of carrying the show. Every appearance is special and memorable.
casting_insights.common_casting: Beautiful sopranos with natural grace and warmth. Often cast with performers who have a genuine quality of kindness.
casting_insights.standout_opportunity: The final scene revelation — 'You've always had the power' — is one of the most beautiful moments in the show when played with genuine warmth.

challenge_areas: Making a brief role feel fully realised
Avoiding one-note sweetness
Creating genuine authority alongside warmth
recommended_for: Sopranos building confidence in named roles
Performers developing stage presence and poise
Those wanting a beautiful role with manageable demands
Young performers stepping up from ensemble

what_directors_look_for: Beautiful, clear soprano voice
Natural warmth and genuine kindness
Grace and poise in movement
Ability to command attention through serenity rather than force
A quality of magic and otherworldliness
common_mistakes: Being so sweet it becomes saccharine
Lacking authority — Glinda is powerful, not just pretty
Flat characterisation — she should feel genuinely magical
Ignoring the wisdom aspect — Glinda knows more than she reveals
tips: Find the mystery in Glinda — she knows Dorothy has the power all along
Warmth and authority are not opposites — embody both
Your entrances are events — prepare for how you arrive onstage
Less is more — a genuine smile from Glinda should light up the theatre

key_songs.title: Come Out, Come Out (Munchkinland)
key_songs.notes: Introduction in Munchkinland. Sets the tone for Glinda's character.

key_songs.title: Glinda's Waltz / Finale
key_songs.notes: Musical underscoring for the ruby slipper revelation. Some versions include a full musical number.

roles.name: The Wizard of Oz / Professor Marvel
roles.description: A humbug showman from Omaha who has been posing as the great and powerful Wizard. The Wizard is all bluster and spectacle hiding a fundamentally decent but cowardly ordinary man. His unmasking is a pivotal moment, and his genuine attempt to help after being exposed reveals his true character. Doubled with Professor Marvel in Kansas.

vocal.style_notes: Two contrasting voices: the booming, amplified Wizard voice and the small, apologetic real voice. Character singing rather than vocal showcase.

dance.notes: Minimal movement required. The role is about vocal and facial acting rather than physical performance.

acting.emotional_range: Wide — bombastic authority to vulnerable honesty to genuine kindness
acting.notes: A masterclass in transitions: the terrifying Wizard voice, the embarrassed unmasking, and the genuine warmth of trying to help. Professor Marvel in Kansas should hint at the Wizard's theatrical nature.

casting_insights.why: A wonderful character role for experienced performers. Limited time commitment but high impact scenes. The unmasking sequence is a beautiful acting moment that showcases range.
casting_insights.common_casting: Experienced character actors with strong vocal presence. Often cast with older, distinguished performers who can play authority convincingly.
casting_insights.standout_opportunity: The unmasking — transitioning from terrifying all-powerful Wizard to embarrassed ordinary man — is a brilliant acting moment.

skills_developed: Playing dual roles with connected characterisation
challenge_areas: Making the transition from Wizard to ordinary man believable
Finding genuine warmth in a fundamentally deceptive character
Connecting Professor Marvel and Wizard characterisations
recommended_for: Experienced actors wanting impactful supporting role
Performers developing voice work and modulation
Character actors seeking a dual-role challenge
Those wanting a significant role with limited rehearsal demands

what_directors_look_for: Strong, commanding vocal presence for the Wizard
Warmth and vulnerability for the unmasked man
Smooth transition between the two modes
Natural authority and theatrical showmanship
Likability despite the character's deception
common_mistakes: Making the Wizard only scary without the showmanship
Not making the unmasked Wizard sympathetic enough
Neglecting Professor Marvel as a separate character
Playing the role too small — the Wizard moments need to be BIG
tips: Professor Marvel should be charming but slightly dodgy — he foreshadows the Wizard
The Wizard voice should be genuinely impressive — practice projection
The unmasking is your Oscar moment — play the embarrassment fully
Genuine kindness in giving the gifts — he really IS trying his best

key_songs.title: Emerald City / Wizard's Entrance
key_songs.notes: Musical underscoring for the reveal. The vocal demands are more about voice acting than singing.

key_songs.title: Balloon Farewell
key_songs.notes: The Wizard's departure. Emotional moment requiring paternal warmth.

roles.name: Auntie Em / Uncle Henry
roles.description: Dorothy's Kansas guardians. Auntie Em is the more prominent of the two — a hardworking, practical farm woman who loves Dorothy deeply but struggles to express it. Uncle Henry is quieter and more supportive. They bookend the show and Dorothy's desire to return to them drives the entire plot. Em's voice calling 'Dorothy!' is a crucial emotional trigger.

vocal.voice_type: Character voices — no major singing required
vocal.tessitura: Speaking roles with minimal singing (ensemble harmonies)
vocal.style_notes: Auntie Em needs a warm, strong speaking voice. Some productions include Em in ensemble singing.

dance.notes: No dance requirements. Natural, grounded movement appropriate for Kansas farm life.

acting.notes: Auntie Em's scenes are few but critical. The opening needs to establish why Dorothy loves her, the crystal ball vision must be heartbreaking, and the finale reunion must be genuinely moving.

special_skills: Establishing strong emotional connection in limited time

casting_insights.why: A small but emotionally important role. Perfect for experienced performers who don't want heavy time commitment but still want to contribute meaningfully. The crystal ball moment and finale are genuinely affecting.
casting_insights.common_casting: Warm, maternal performers for Em. Reliable character actors for Henry.
casting_insights.standout_opportunity: The crystal ball scene — Em calling out to Dorothy — can be devastating when played with genuine love and fear.

challenge_areas: Creating full character in very limited stage time
Making Kansas feel real and worth returning to
recommended_for: Performers wanting manageable time commitment
Actors building confidence in named roles
Those developing emotional authenticity

what_directors_look_for: Warmth and genuine maternal/paternal quality
Ability to establish deep relationship with Dorothy quickly
Grounded, authentic presence
Emotional availability for key moments
common_mistakes: Playing Em as cold or dismissive in opening scenes
Not investing enough because the role is small
Forgetting that Dorothy's love for Em drives the ENTIRE plot
tips: Every moment Em has with Dorothy must radiate love — even when she's busy or worried
The crystal ball moment is your star turn — make it count
Dorothy wants to come HOME — make home feel like somewhere worth returning to

key_songs.title: Kansas scenes
key_songs.notes: Primarily acting scenes with musical underscoring.

roles.name: Ensemble (Munchkins / Emerald City Citizens / Winkies / Flying Monkeys)
roles.description: The Wizard of Oz ensemble creates multiple distinct worlds: the cheerful Munchkins of Munchkinland, the elegant citizens of Emerald City, the Witch's fearsome Winkies/guards, and the Flying Monkeys. Many productions also use child ensembles for Munchkins. The ensemble transforms between these groups, creating the magical variety of Oz.

vocal.tessitura: Varies by section — Munchkins often higher/lighter, guards lower/darker
vocal.style_notes: Strong choral singing for Munchkinland ('Ding Dong the Witch is Dead'), Emerald City ('Merry Old Land of Oz'), and guard chant ('O-Ee-Yah! Eoh-Ah!'). Must adapt vocal color to each world.

dance.stamina: High — multiple transformations and group numbers
dance.notes: Each ensemble group has distinct movement vocabulary: Munchkins are small and lively, Emerald City citizens are elegant, Winkies are military and menacing, Flying Monkeys are acrobatic/athletic.

acting.emotional_range: Varies by scene — joyful, fearful, celebratory, menacing
acting.notes: Must create distinct characters for each world. Munchkins need individual personality, Winkies need genuine menace, Emerald City citizens need sophistication.

casting_insights.why: The Oz ensemble is uniquely varied — you play 3-4 completely different groups in one show. This builds versatility, quick-change skills, and the ability to create distinct characters rapidly. Great training ground.
casting_insights.common_casting: Versatile performers of all ages. Child ensembles common for Munchkins. Need strong singers and movers who can transform between worlds.
casting_insights.standout_opportunity: Individual Munchkin characters can be scene-stealers. The 'Ding Dong' sequence often features fun solo moments within the ensemble.

challenge_areas: Managing multiple costumes and quick changes
Switching character completely between scenes
Maintaining energy across varied ensemble roles
recommended_for: New performers getting first musical experience
Young performers (especially Munchkins)
Versatile performers who enjoy variety
Those building foundational ensemble skills

what_directors_look_for: Versatility and willingness to play multiple roles
Strong choral singing voice
Physical expressiveness
Ability to create distinct characters quickly
Reliability and team spirit
common_mistakes: Playing all ensemble roles the same way
Not committing to the world-building in each scene
Underestimating quick-change demands
Fading into the background instead of creating character
tips: Create a specific character for each world — give each one a name and story
Practice quick changes at home — speed and organization matter
'Ding Dong the Witch is Dead' is one of the most fun ensemble numbers ever — bring the joy!
The Winkie march is menacing — commit fully to the military precision
